# Density matrix basics

## Why a new description?

{{< include /_macros.qmd >}}

State vectors cannot describe:

- **Uncertainty about** which state a system is in ("$\ket0$ or $\ket+$, each with probability ½").
- **Part of an entangled system**, such as one qubit of an e-bit.
- **Noisy** processes that are not unitary.

. . .

The **density matrix** handles all three, and contains state vectors as a special case:

$$
\ket\psi\quad\longrightarrow\quad\rho=\ket\psi\bra\psi .
$$

## Definition

::: {.box}
[Density matrix]{.box-title}
A square complex matrix $\rho$ with

1. **unit trace**: $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=1$, and
2. **positive semidefinite**: $\rho\ge0$.
:::

- **Trace**: sum of diagonal entries; linear, and $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$.
- **Positive semidefinite** (equivalent forms): $\rho=M^\dagger M$ for some $M$; Hermitian with nonnegative eigenvalues; $\bra\psi\rho\ket\psi\ge0$ for every $\ket\psi$.

. . .

For $\rho=\ket\psi\bra\psi$: $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\braket\psi\psi=1$ and $\bra\phi\rho\ket\phi=\abs{\braket\phi\psi}^2\ge0$. ✓

## Reading a density matrix

$$
\rho=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac34&\tfrac14\\[1mm]\tfrac14&\tfrac14\end{pmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{array}{l}
\text{diagonal: probabilities of a standard basis measurement}\\[1mm]
\text{off-diagonal: coherence (needed for interference)}
\end{array}
$$

- Standard basis measurement: outcome $a$ with probability $\bra a\rho\ket a$.
- Unitary $U$: $\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger$.
- **Global phases disappear**: $e^{i\theta}\ket\psi$ and $\ket\psi$ give the same $\ket\psi\bra\psi$. One representation per physical state.

::: {.aside-note}
A density matrix is **pure** if $\rho=\ket\psi\bra\psi$, i.e. rank one. Otherwise it is **mixed**.
:::

# Convex combinations

## Probabilistic selections

Prepare $\rho_0$ with probability $p_0$, …, $\rho_{m-1}$ with probability $p_{m-1}$. The resulting state is the **convex combination**

$$
\rho=\sum_k p_k\rho_k .
$$

All measurement statistics are the averages of those for each $\rho_k$, so nothing else is needed.

. . .

$$
\tfrac12\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket+\bra+=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac34&\tfrac14\\[1mm]\tfrac14&\tfrac14\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Different mixtures can give the **same** density matrix, and then they are indistinguishable. Example: $\tfrac12\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket1\bra1=\tfrac12\ket+\bra++\tfrac12\ket-\bra-$.

## The completely mixed state

$$
\frac{\mathbb I}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{a}\ket a\bra a=\frac1n\sum_{k}\ket{\psi_k}\bra{\psi_k}
\quad\text{for any orthonormal basis }\{\ket{\psi_k}\}.
$$

- Every measurement in every basis gives uniformly random outcomes.
- It represents **total uncertainty**: the quantum analogue of a uniformly random classical state.

. . .

**Classical probabilistic states** are the **diagonal** density matrices:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}p_0\\\vdots\\p_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\sum_a p_a\ket a\bra a .
$$

## Spectral decomposition

Every density matrix is a mixture of **orthogonal pure states**:

$$
\rho=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\lambda_k\ket{\psi_k}\bra{\psi_k},
\qquad \lambda_k\ge0,\ \ \sum_k\lambda_k=1 .
$$

(Spectral theorem; positive semidefinite $\Rightarrow\lambda_k\ge0$; trace one $\Rightarrow\sum\lambda_k=1$.)

. . .

For the example above: eigenvalues $\cos^2(\pi/8)\approx0.854$ and $\sin^2(\pi/8)\approx0.146$, with eigenvectors $\ket{\psi_{\pi/8}}$ and $\ket{\psi_{5\pi/8}}$, where $\ket{\psi_\theta}=\cos\theta\ket0+\sin\theta\ket1$.

# The Bloch sphere

## Qubit states as points

Every qubit density matrix can be written with a vector $(r_x,r_y,r_z)$ of length $\le1$:

$$
\rho=\frac{\mathbb I+r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z}{2}
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+r_z&r_x-ir_y\\r_x+ir_y&1-r_z\end{pmatrix}.
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](../figures/six-Bloch-sphere-points.avif){width="82%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
- **Pure states** lie on the surface ($\norm r=1$); mixed states inside.
- $\ket0,\ket1$: poles. $\ket\pm$: $\pm x$. $\ket{\pm i}$: $\pm y$.
- Orthogonal states are **antipodal**.
- The center is $\mathbb I/2$.
- Eigenvalues of $\rho$: $\tfrac{1\pm\norm r}{2}$.
:::
::::

## Mixtures are straight lines

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](../figures/Bloch-sphere-zero-plus-average.avif){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
The map $\rho\leftrightarrow r$ is **affine**, so a mixture of states is the same mixture of points.

$\tfrac12\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket+\bra+$ is the midpoint of the chord from $\ket0$ to $\ket+$.

The same point is also on the diameter from $\ket{\psi_{\pi/8}}$ to $\ket{\psi_{5\pi/8}}$: its spectral decomposition.
:::
::::

## Try it: a qubit density matrix {.scrollable}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rlen = Inputs.range([0, 1], {step: 0.01, value: 0.71, label: "length ‖r‖"})
viewof th = Inputs.range([0, 180], {step: 1, value: 45, label: "θ from +z (degrees)"})
viewof ph = Inputs.range([0, 360], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "φ from +x (degrees)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dm = {
  const t = th * Math.PI / 180, p = ph * Math.PI / 180;
  const rx = rlen * Math.sin(t) * Math.cos(p), ry = rlen * Math.sin(t) * Math.sin(p), rz = rlen * Math.cos(t);
  const f = x => (Math.abs(x) < 5e-4 ? 0 : x).toFixed(3);
  const c = (re, im) => `${f(re)}${im < 0 ? " − " : " + "}${f(Math.abs(im))}i`;
  return {rx, ry, rz, f, c, l0: (1 + rlen) / 2, l1: (1 - rlen) / 2, purity: (1 + rlen * rlen) / 2};
}
html`<table style="font-size:0.75em;border-collapse:collapse">
<tr><td style="padding:2px 18px">ρ =</td>
<td style="border-left:2px solid currentColor;border-right:2px solid currentColor;padding:4px 12px;font-family:monospace">
${dm.f((1 + dm.rz) / 2)} &nbsp; ${dm.c(dm.rx / 2, -dm.ry / 2)}<br>${dm.c(dm.rx / 2, dm.ry / 2)} &nbsp; ${dm.f((1 - dm.rz) / 2)}</td>
<td style="padding:2px 18px">eigenvalues ${dm.f(dm.l0)}, ${dm.f(dm.l1)}<br>Tr(ρ²) = ${dm.f(dm.purity)} ${rlen > 0.999 ? "(pure)" : rlen < 0.001 ? "(completely mixed)" : "(mixed)"}</td></tr></table>`
```

Defaults: the example $\tfrac12\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket+\bra+$ ($\norm r=1/\sqrt2$, $\theta=45^\circ$). Set the length to $1$ for a pure state, $0$ for $\mathbb I/2$.

# Multiple systems

## Product, correlated and entangled states

- **Product state**: $\rho\otimes\sigma$, for independent systems.
- **Correlated (classical)**: $\tfrac12\ket0\bra0\otimes\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket1\bra1\otimes\ket1\bra1$.
- **Entangled**: $\ket{\phi^+}\bra{\phi^+}$, which is **not** a mixture of product states.

. . .

::: {.box}
[Separable vs. entangled]{.box-title}
A state is **separable** if it is a convex combination of product states $\sum_k p_k\,\rho_k\otimes\sigma_k$. Otherwise it is **entangled**.
:::

## Reduced states and the partial trace

What is the state of $\mathsf X$ alone, when $(\mathsf X,\mathsf Y)$ is in $\rho$? Average over everything $\mathsf Y$ could do:

$$
\rho_{\mathsf X}=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf Y}(\rho),
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf Y}\bigl(A\otimes B\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}(B)\,A,\ \text{extended linearly.}
$$

. . .

**An e-bit:**

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf Y}\bigl(\ket{\phi^+}\bra{\phi^+}\bigr)=\tfrac12\ket0\bra0+\tfrac12\ket1\bra1=\frac{\mathbb I}{2}.
$$

Each half of an e-bit, on its own, is **completely mixed**: a maximally entangled pure state has maximally mixed parts.

::: {.notes}
Concretely: $\ket{\phi^+}\bra{\phi^+}=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}\ket a\bra b\otimes\ket a\bra b$.
The partial trace keeps $\ket a\bra b\cdot\operatorname{Tr}(\ket a\bra b)$, which is
zero unless $a=b$. Alternative description: $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf Y}(\rho)=\sum_b(\mathbb I\otimes\bra b)\rho(\mathbb I\otimes\ket b)$.
:::

## The partial trace for two qubits

Write $\rho$ in $2\times2$ blocks (rows and columns ordered $00,01,10,11$, with $\mathsf X$ first):

$$
\rho=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf X}(\rho)=A+D,
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathsf Y}(\rho)=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Tr}A&\operatorname{Tr}B\\\operatorname{Tr}C&\operatorname{Tr}D\end{pmatrix}.
$$

. . .

In Qiskit:

```python
from qiskit.quantum_info import DensityMatrix, partial_trace
rho = DensityMatrix.from_label("00")          # any 2-qubit state
partial_trace(rho, [1])                       # trace out qubit 1, keep qubit 0
```

## Recap

1. A **density matrix** is positive semidefinite with trace one; $\ket\psi\mapsto\ket\psi\bra\psi$ embeds pure states.
2. **Mixtures** are convex combinations. Different mixtures can give the same $\rho$, and then they cannot be told apart.
3. $\mathbb I/n$ is **completely mixed**; diagonal density matrices are classical probabilistic states.
4. Qubit states form the **Bloch ball**: pure on the surface, mixtures along chords.
5. The **partial trace** gives the state of a subsystem; each half of an e-bit is $\mathbb I/2$.
